nameStory: The "ursine" in this beetle's name comes from the Latin word for "bear," likely referring to its stocky, rounded shape that resembles a tiny bear when viewed from above. The "spurleg" part refers to a characteristic feature of this genus - small spines or spurs on their legs that help them grip surfaces while hunting for prey.
description: The Ursine Spurleg is a small lady beetle that's quite different from the classic red-and-black ladybugs most people know. These tiny predators are typically black or dark brown with distinctive orange or yellow spots scattered across their wing covers. They're among the smaller lady beetles you'll encounter in New England, with a compact, rounded body that's perfectly designed for squeezing into tight spaces while hunting for aphids and other small insects.

idTips.label: Orange spots on dark background
idTips.description: Look for bright orange or yellow-orange spots against a black or very dark brown background - the reverse pattern of common red ladybugs

idTips.label: Small, compact size
idTips.description: Noticeably smaller and more rounded than typical ladybugs, feeling almost bead-like if gently handled

idTips.label: Leg spurs
idTips.description: Tiny spines visible on the legs when viewed with a magnifying glass - these give the spurleg beetles their name

idTips.label: Smooth, glossy surface
idTips.description: Wing covers have a hard, shiny finish that reflects light, feeling slick to the touch like a polished stone

habitat: Look for Ursine Spurlegs in gardens, parks, and forest edges where aphids and scale insects are abundant. They're often found on flowering plants, shrubs, and trees where they hunt for soft-bodied prey. You might spot them crawling on roses, fruit trees, or ornamental plants, especially in areas with mixed vegetation and good sun exposure.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge from winter hiding spots and become active as temperatures warm, often seen on early flowering plants hunting for aphids.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible, actively feeding and mating on a variety of plants throughout gardens and natural areas.
seasonality.fall: Adults continue feeding to build up energy reserves before winter, often congregating on late-season flowers and seed heads.
seasonality.winter: Adults hibernate under bark, leaf litter, or in other protected locations, remaining hidden until spring warmth returns.

funFact: Unlike many lady beetles that overwinter in large groups under rocks or logs, Ursine Spurlegs often squeeze into incredibly tight spaces like bark crevices barely wider than their own bodies, using their leg spurs like tiny climbing spikes to wedge themselves securely in place.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small, dark lady beetles, but the orange-on-black color pattern is distinctive - remember "reverse ladybug" since most familiar ladybugs are red or orange with black spots, not the other way around.
contextualKnowledge: Many people don't realize that lady beetles come in colors other than the classic red with black spots, so this species often surprises observers who assume all "ladybugs" look the same.
compareHints: This is the only Brachiacantha species regularly found in New England, making it unique among spurleg lady beetles in the region. Compared to other small lady beetles in different genera, the Ursine Spurleg's orange-spotted pattern and leg spurs set it apart from similarly-sized species that typically have different spot arrangements or lack the characteristic leg spines.
